title: Industry Pulse — AI / Agent Ecosystem

bullets.title: Claude Code 2.1.248 shipped `--restricted` — a mode that REMOVES the command-running tools instead of asking permission for them, which is the first STRUCTURAL answer to the credentialed-unattended-agent problem this report has tracked for three weeks
bullets.summary: Verified against the canonical CHANGELOG.md, not a summary of it: `--restricted` (or `CLAUDE_CODE_RESTRICTED=1`) removes the built-in tools that run commands or code and removes `WebFetch` unless it is named in `--tools`, keeps file tools inside the working directory, refuses `bypassPermissions`, and ignores user, project and local settings files. Two further 2.1.248 entries land on the same automation surface: `claude self-hosted-runner --client-label <label>` overrides the label the runner registers with, and server-managed settings diagnostics now emit a startup warning plus a `/doctor` and `/status` line when settings fail to load or were never fetched — the failure reasons named explicitly are Bedrock/Vertex/third-party provider and a custom `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`. `/usage-credits` arrives for Enterprise orgs billed through AWS Marketplace, and cross-session `SendMessage`/`ListAgents` now works on Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry and with telemetry disabled. 2.1.250 is the newest entry on the changelog and is bug fixes only.
bullets.how: YES, and it is the most useful item this report has surfaced for the Hermes design in a month. `2.1.248`, `2.1.250`, `CLAUDE_CODE_RESTRICTED`, `cacheTtl` and `usage-credits` all return ZERO matches across the corpus; Releasebot's newest entry is still 2.1.247, so this was read off the vendor's own file rather than a mirror — which is exactly the discipline yesterday's scan wrote down. The reason it matters is specific. Every permission item this report has logged since 08-07 — the 2.1.223 evaluated-string bypass, the dangling `&&`/`||` approval fix, the ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL telemetry leak — has been a patch narrowing the gap between what the permission system checks and what the shell runs. `--restricted` does not narrow that gap; it deletes the surface. For a scheduled loop that only reads the public web and writes files into one repo — which describes this Pulse scan, the Lens sweep, the answer-page checks and most of the daily fleet — the shell tools are not a capability that needs guarding, they are dead weight with a blast radius. The clause that makes it load-bearing rather than cosmetic is "ignores user, project and local settings files": a mode that cannot be widened by editing a settings file is a different security object from a mode that merely defaults to narrow, and that distinction is the whole argument for using it on unattended jobs. Two honest caveats. First, `--restricted` also removes `WebFetch` unless named in `--tools`, so a research loop must opt its fetch tool back in explicitly — this is a per-loop configuration change, not a global flag anyone should flip across the fleet in one pass. Second, nobody here has run it; the changelog states behaviour, it does not verify it in Bobby's build. The action is one scoped experiment on a single read-only loop, not a migration. The server-managed settings diagnostics are the small companion win: the fleet has repeatedly failed silently on config, and a `/doctor` line that names the reason converts a silent wrong result into a visible one.

bullets.title: The SAME release quietly closed a credential EXFILTRATION path — `/ultrareview` and cloud sessions were uploading uncommitted `prod.env`-style files, `*.tfvars`, and editor swap and backup copies of keys like `key.pem.tmp` and `id_rsa.swo` — the second consecutive day of credential-scoping fixes
bullets.summary: The 2.1.248 entry reads: fixed `/ultrareview` and locally seeded cloud sessions uploading uncommitted edits to `prod.env`-style and `*.tfvars` files, or to editor swap, temp, and backup copies of credential files (e.g. `key.pem.tmp`, `id_rsa.swo`); they now stay on the machine. Three more entries in the same version touch unattended and desktop work directly. Claude Desktop and Cowork sessions were disappearing after 30 days — transcript cleanup now keeps desktop-written sessions while they are in the app, with a new `desktopSessionCleanupPeriodDays` setting capping the exemption. A background session with a `PermissionRequest` or `PreToolUse` hook that prints an invalid answer used to wait silently; the `claude agents` row now names the hook and the schema error. And a backgrounded worktree session now holds the worktree's lock while it runs, so cleanup and `git worktree remove` leave it alone. On cost, `experimental.cacheTtl` (`"5m"` or `"1h"`) is now settable per agent in frontmatter, and the Workflow tool's description dropped from about 5.7k tokens to about 1k with the script-writing reference moved into a bundled `workflow-authoring` skill.
bullets.how: YES, and the exfiltration fix is the one to actually check. `ultrareview`, `tfvars`, `workflow-authoring` and `desktopSessionCleanupPeriodDays` all return zero corpus matches. Yesterday's finding was that telemetry was sending a gateway's API key to the wrong host; today's is that a review command was sending uncommitted secret-adjacent files off the machine. Neither is a breach here and neither should be treated as one — but the pattern across two consecutive releases is that the leak path was a legitimate feature reading more of the working directory than its purpose required, which is precisely the failure class an environment full of SSH keys, deploy credentials and `.env` files is exposed to. The concrete check is small and bounded: has anyone run `/ultrareview` or seeded a cloud session from a directory that holds DreamHost or GitHub credentials, and is the fleet past 2.1.248. Fold it into the version-and-config check already carried and unresolved from the last two days — past 2.1.223, past 2.1.246, past 2.1.248, no wildcard before a Bash subcommand, and whether any machine sets `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`. That is now one task with four checkboxes, not four tasks, and it has been open long enough to be the most overdue item in this corpus. The Cowork 30-day fix is worth naming separately because it is invisible until it costs something: Bobby's daily loops are Cowork sessions, and a transcript quietly deleted at day 30 is history this report's own continuity depends on. The two cost items pair with yesterday's `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_MODEL` and the per-loop `/usage` panel — the fleet now has three independent cost levers logged in three days and has pulled none of them.

bullets.title: CORRECTION — yesterday's falsification step KILLED a real feature: `SendFeedback` shipped in 2.1.247, and this report rejected it because a search summary had dressed it in a fabricated filesystem path
bullets.summary: Yesterday's bullet 4 recorded a kill: a search summary claimed that on August 27 Claude Code announced it now writes its own feedback reports, with drafts queued locally in `~/.claude/feedback/drafts/` until sent, and the scan rejected the whole item after finding nothing on the vendor's release surfaces. Read directly today, the 2.1.247 entry — first seen by Releasebot on Aug 27, and present in the canonical CHANGELOG — says: "Added the `SendFeedback` tool: when something goes wrong in a session, Claude can draft a feedback report for you to review and send from `/feedback` (turn off with the `feedbackDrafts` setting)." The capability is real, the date is right, and the mechanism is right. The only false element was the invented directory path. The rest of 2.1.247 was also missed and is worth naming: `/claude-api cost-optimize` profiles an existing project's API spend and works through caching, token hygiene, batch, effort and model choice one measured change at a time; terminal hyperlinks in rendered markdown that point at a network or automounter path, contain a control character, or lead with an invisible character now render as plain text; plugin marketplace names containing control or invisible characters are rejected; and on Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry and telemetry-disabled sessions Claude is now TOLD when a configured MCP server failed to connect instead of concluding its tools do not exist.
bullets.how: YES, and this is the most valuable entry today because it corrects this report rather than the world. Yesterday's lesson — "a summary of a source is not the source" — was right and stays. What it missed is the failure mode on the other side: the summary was mostly TRUE, and the scan threw out a true claim because one specific attached to it was false. Falsification has to separate the claim from its ornament. The correct verdict yesterday was "feature confirmed, path unverified and probably invented," which is a shipped bullet with a caveat, not a kill. A report that only guards against false positives will accumulate false negatives instead, and a false negative is harder to catch precisely because nothing enters the corpus to later contradict. The concrete rule: when a source summary contains several claims, verify each independently and report the surviving subset — do not let one bad detail take the rest with it. On substance, two 2.1.247 items are directly applicable. The MCP connection-failure notice is the fix for a failure this environment produces constantly — this very session opened with sixteen servers needing authentication and several still connecting, and a model that silently concludes a tool does not exist will confidently report a capability gap that is really an auth gap. And the terminal-hyperlink hardening is prompt-injection defence in the exact shape this stack is exposed to: an agent that reads scraped web pages and renders markdown into a terminal.

bullets.title: CORPUS GAP — general contractors' full project record is now agent-queryable over MCP: Constructable exposes drawings, RFIs, submittals, daily logs, change events, financials and quality lists to Claude and ChatGPT, aimed squarely at the $20M–$150M GC that is Brand 9's actual buyer
bullets.summary: Verified by reading the vendor's own page rather than a search summary. Constructable, a Y Combinator construction-management product built for mid-size general contractors running $20M to $150M in annual volume, ships a native remote MCP server at `https://api.constructable.ai/mcp` that exposes the core project record — drawings, RFIs, submittals, daily logs, change events, financials and quality lists — to any MCP-compatible client, with a listed ChatGPT App and step-by-step Claude custom-connector instructions. It offers write access as well as read, and the vendor's own setup guidance recommends setting read-only tools to "Always Allow" while leaving write and delete tools on "Needs Approval." Pricing is flat-fee with unlimited users, explicitly so external AI tools can draw on the same project data without per-seat cost. The post is dated July 6, 2026 and titled for June 2026 — this is a corpus gap, not today's news, and it is logged with that stated plainly.
bullets.how: YES for Brand 9, and it is the first construction-side MCP this corpus has ever carried: `Constructable` returns zero matches across every file, while the adjacent verticals this report already logged — Green Street for commercial real estate, Rechat for residential, and the CastHub/Screenly/Revel Digital digital-signage servers — are all carried and suppressed today. The gap matters because those three were all one step away from Bobby's business, and this one is not. Brand 9 sells into homebuilders and general contractors; ATLAS exists because Lennar sign operations is a tracking problem across communities, permits, install crews and status. The objects Constructable exposes are the objects a sign scope actually lives inside: a submittal is where a monument sign spec gets approved, a change event is where a wayfinding revision becomes billable, and a daily log is where an install date is really recorded. Three reads, in descending confidence. First and most solid: this is evidence for the PRAGMA pitch, because a GC whose project record is already agent-queryable is a buyer who has stopped needing to be convinced that agents belong in construction — the education cost is gone, and the conversation starts at what to point the agent at. Second: the vendor's own read-allow / write-approve recommendation is the same permission posture this report has been arguing for all week, arrived at independently by a construction vendor, which is a small confirmation that the boundary convention is converging rather than being invented here. Third and most speculative, flagged as such: if a builder client ever runs Constructable, a sign vendor with read access to the submittal and change-event stream would know about a scope change before the email arrives — that is a real advantage and it is entirely hypothetical, since nobody has confirmed a single B9 client uses this product. The honest status is a capability to hold and a question to ask a builder contact, not a build.

bullets.title: Frontier flat for the FIFTEENTH consecutive scan — and an anonymous "OX Alpha" model beating GPT-5.6 on coding benchmarks was refused for lack of attribution
bullets.summary: No frontier lab — OpenAI, Google, Meta, Mistral, xAI, DeepSeek or Cohere — shipped a model or material availability change in this window. GLM-5.2 Turbo from Z.AI (Aug 17) remains the most recent entry; Gemini 3.7 Flash (Aug 13) is Google's newest and is already carried, and OpenAI's flagship line is still the July GPT-5.6 Sol/Luna/Terra tracks with Luna the free-tier default. One candidate was refused rather than killed: a tracker summary describes an "OX Alpha" model outperforming GPT-5.6 on coding benchmarks with production adoption inside 24 hours and a free preview ending around Aug 27, while stating that official attribution has not been confirmed and the creator remains anonymous. An unattributed frontier-class model is not a reportable release, and it is recorded here as seen-and-refused so a later scan does not rediscover it as new. Suppressed as already carried: the entire agent-funding slate (Instinct's $250M at $2.5B, HappyRobot's $150M at $1.2B, Zenity's $125M, Cognition at $40B-plus); every adjacent MCP item that resurfaced this window — X Ads' 23-tool server from 08-25, the CastHub/Screenly/Revel Digital signage servers, Green Street, Rechat, and the MCP 2026-07-28 stateless/OAuth/OIDC spec work; and arXiv 2607.08028 "From Prompts to Contracts: Harness Engineering for Auditable Enterprise LLM Agents," carried since 07-14.
bullets.how: MAYBE, and the refusal is the part worth keeping. "Beats GPT-5.6, anonymous creator, preview ending imminently" has the exact shape of a claim that is interesting enough to repeat and impossible to check, and the corpus already carries the cost of that mistake twice — the fabricated feedback path yesterday and the false signage-MCP negative that survived weeks. Refusing on attribution rather than on plausibility is the cheaper rule, because plausibility is what makes these items dangerous in the first place. On substance, fifteen flat scans is now more than two consecutive months in which the ecosystem's news has been permission modes, credential scoping, cost levers, governance gateways and vertical MCP coverage — not capability. Today makes that unusually clean: the single most consequential item in this scan is a flag that DELETES tools, and the second is a fix that stops a feature reading files it did not need. That is what a maturing platform's news looks like, and it is the entire PRAGMA argument stated by the market — when nobody can differentiate on model access, the defensible layer is proprietary data and governed delivery, which is what the AAIR score history, the answer-page corpus and the attribution chain are. The suppression list is itself a signal worth noting: four separate MCP stories resurfaced in this window and every one was already in the corpus, which means the thread is now running ahead of the coverage rather than behind it.

praxis_lesson: Falsification has to separate a claim from its ornament. Yesterday this report killed a Claude Code feature because a search summary attached a fabricated filesystem path to it — and the feature was real, shipping as the `SendFeedback` tool in 2.1.247. The correct verdict was "confirmed, path unverified," a shipped bullet with a caveat, not a kill. Guarding only against false positives quietly manufactures false negatives, and a false negative is worse because nothing enters the corpus to later contradict it: verify each claim in a summary independently and report the subset that survives. The day's largest item is structural rather than procedural. Claude Code 2.1.248 shipped `--restricted`, which does not narrow the gap between what the permission system evaluates and what the shell executes — it removes the shell tools entirely, locks file tools to the working directory, refuses `bypassPermissions`, and, critically, ignores user, project and local settings files, so the mode cannot be widened by editing a file. For unattended loops that only read the public web and write into one repo — this scan, the Lens sweep, the answer-page checks, most of the daily fleet — the command tools are not a guarded capability, they are blast radius with no upside. Run one scoped experiment on a single read-only loop before touching anything else, and remember `WebFetch` must be opted back in via `--tools`. The same release closed a credential-exfiltration path, with `/ultrareview` and cloud sessions uploading uncommitted `prod.env`-style files, `*.tfvars`, and swap and backup copies of keys — the second consecutive day of credential-scoping fixes, in an environment full of SSH and deploy credentials. One task, four checkboxes. Meanwhile the frontier is flat for the fifteenth consecutive scan, and the corpus gap worth closing is commercial rather than technical: Constructable exposes a general contractor's drawings, RFIs, submittals, change events and daily logs over MCP to mid-size GCs — the exact buyer Brand 9 sells into, and the exact objects a sign scope lives inside.
